questions.question: A team breaks a feature into six tickets: schema, pipeline, service, API, interface, polish. Each is small, estimated, and reviewable. What is the defect?
options: The tickets are too large and should be split further
The order is wrong; polish should come before the interface
The breakdown follows the architecture, so all learning and all integration risk land in the final week
Nothing is wrong; the pieces come together at the launch date, which is when the feature becomes real
questions.explanation: Smaller is not the same as sliced. Nothing finished early can be shown, tested, or kept, and the pieces only meet once. Option D is the most tempting because it matches how most calendars are drawn: it treats launch as a single dated event, which is exactly what pushes all learning and all integration risk into the week with the least room to respond. Option A is the wrong axis, since splitting the schema ticket in half changes nothing about when the team learns.

questions.question: Your feature needs an identity service that another team owns and has not built yet. How should this dependency be handled?
options: Write an interface contract and build against a stub, because this is a capability dependency
Sequence your work after their delivery date, because you cannot build on something that does not exist
Open a bounded investigation with a decision date, because the shape of the work is unknown
Escalate to leadership so their team is re-prioritized to unblock you
questions.explanation: A capability dependency needs a contract and a stub so both sides can move. Option B is the tempting one and the most common error in practice: it reads as realistic sequencing, but it converts another team's schedule into your critical path for no reason. Option C misreads a capability dependency as a knowledge dependency; you know what you need, you just do not have it yet.

questions.question: A dependency migration has a moment where the old system stops and the new one starts. A PM insists on slicing that moment into three incremental steps. What is the likely result?
options: Lower risk, since incremental change is always safer than a single switch
Dual-running complexity that can be riskier than one rehearsed switch
Slower delivery but strictly better evidence about the migration
No change, since the cutover is atomic in the database regardless
questions.explanation: This is the floor of the slicing model. You can slice preparation, compatibility, verification, rehearsal, and rollback readiness, but not the moment itself. Option A is the belief that makes competent teams do this: incrementalism is usually safer, and here it means maintaining two live paths, which is its own failure surface.

questions.question: Engineering estimates a migration at three to five weeks against a ten-week deadline. Which first slice best fits the sequencing rule?
options: The largest module, so the bulk of the work is behind you early
The lowest-risk module, so the team builds confidence and momentum
The module the team has already scoped, so the first slice finishes predictably
The part that contains the reason the estimate spans two weeks, so the spread narrows
questions.explanation: Order by which uncertainty is most expensive to discover late. With a ten-week horizon and a two-week spread, the spread itself is the thing to attack first. Option A is the answer that sounds like progress and is the most tempting: it moves the most work, but if the unknown part turns out to be the five-week end, you find out in week six with nothing left to trade.

questions.question: A team ships thin vertical slices every few days. Nobody looks at what a slice produced before the next one starts. What does the team have?
options: A working sequence; evidence accumulates and can be reviewed at the end
Smaller tickets with a better name, because a slice yields evidence only when someone asks a question of it
A risk-shaped sequence, since vertical slicing reduces integration risk by itself
An option-value problem, because partial slices cannot be kept
questions.explanation: Evidence yield is a property of the review, not of the slice shape. Option A is the honest-sounding trap: reviewing at the end is exactly the pattern vertical slicing was meant to replace, and by then no slice can change the next one. Option C is partly true — integration safety does improve — but it is not what the question asks about, and it does not restore the lost learning.
